book.author: Robin S. Sharma

facts: Sharma's book is a fable: John hears his former mentor Julian Mantle describe what he learned from the Sages of Sivana in the Himalayas.
John's father had told him: 'John, on your deathbed you will never wish you spent more time at the office.' John began spending a little more time at home.
About six months after Julian arrived in Sivana, Divea, the youngest sage, came to his hut with a gift from all the sages: a miniature hourglass of blown glass and a small piece of sandalwood.
Each sage had received one as a child; though they owned nothing, the hourglasses were daily reminders of mortality and of living full days.
In Yogi Raman's fable a gold stopwatch stands for time, which 'slips through our hands like grains of sand'.
Divea's advice: the best time to plant a tree was forty years ago; the second best time is today. 'Develop a deathbed mentality.'

Julian: ask yourself each day 'What would I do today if it was my last?'; you start on the meaningful things you've been putting off. John calls it morbid; Julian answers that it is a philosophy about life.
The chapter's techniques also include having the courage to say 'no'.

lessons.idea: Use the deathbed question on one ordinary day to find the thing you keep postponing, then do it today.
lessons.anchor: Divea's hourglass and the question 'What would I do today if it was my last?'

reflect_final: What meaningful thing have you postponed for so long that you no longer notice you are postponing it?

use_cases.move: In Sharma's fable each monk kept a small hourglass. Let's each pick one thing we've kept putting off and do it this weekend.

use_cases.situation: Friend says they'll call their parent 'when things calm down'
use_cases.move: Ask what would happen if they called this evening instead.
Put the thing you've postponed longest at the top and say no to one smaller task.

pocket_idea: The sages kept hourglasses to see time pass; name one postponed thing and do it before the sand runs out today.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Monks who owned nothing still each kept a little hourglass.
